record.original_question: Define and study symmetry for random strings and random sequences, and determine whether lack of symmetry should be regarded as evidence of non-randomness.

evidence.quote: 19. Define and study the symmetry of random strings and sequences. Is the absence of symmetry a symptom of non-randomness? (C. Calude)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. In algorithmic information theory, a binary string x ∈ {0,1}* is called (Kolmogorov–Chaitin) random if its prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity satisfies H(x) ≥ |x| − c for some constant c, and an infinite binary sequence x ∈ {0,1}^ω is called (Martin-Löf / Chaitin) random if there exists a constant c such that H(x ↾ n) ≥ n − c for all n, equivalently if it passes every Martin-Löf test.

Informally, a string or sequence is said to exhibit a "symmetry" when it is invariant under some nontrivial transformation, e.g. reversal, complementation (0 ↔ 1), cyclic shift, a permutation of positions in a fixed group, a self-similarity / repetition pattern, or, more generally, a computable bijection T : {0,1}^* → {0,1}^* (resp. T : {0,1}^ω → {0,1}^ω) such that T(x) = x.

Problem. 
(a) Propose a precise, mathematically robust definition of "symmetry" for finite binary strings and for infinite binary sequences, broad enough to encompass natural examples (reversal-invariance, complementation-invariance, periodicity, invariance under finite permutation groups, and invariance under prescribed classes of computable transformations) yet refined enough to be nontrivial for random objects.

(b) Develop a theory of such symmetries: for each chosen notion of symmetry S, characterize the class of strings/sequences that possess S, study the Kolmogorov complexity (or initial-segment complexity) of S-symmetric objects, and quantify how many random strings of length n possess S.

(c) Decide the following question: if a finite string x (resp. an infinite sequence x) possesses a nontrivial symmetry in the sense of (a), must this be regarded as evidence of non-randomness? Concretely, is it true that the existence of a nontrivial symmetry implies that x cannot be Kolmogorov–Chaitin random (in the finite case, up to an additive constant) or Martin-Löf random (in the infinite case)? If not, exhibit symmetric random objects; if yes, prove the implication and quantify the resulting complexity deficiency.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears in a well-known list of open problems in algorithmic information theory (compiled by C. Calude), and no published resolution defining a general theory of symmetry for random strings/sequences and settling whether absence of symmetry is a symptom of non-randomness has been located. Related work (e.g. on transformations preserving randomness, and on algorithmic complexity over symmetry classes) exists, but does not provide a definitive answer to the question as posed.
